name: Homosalate

lead: Homosalate is a chemical sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB light and is used to build SPF. It is reported in roughly 45% of US sunscreens.
European regulators have examined it for hormone-like effects seen in lab assays. Summaries disagree on how firm the concern is, and no human harm has been demonstrated in the studies listed.

paras: Its salicylate group absorbs UVB and its bulky ring keeps it from washing out in water [2].

It is absorbed into blood after sunscreen use per a 2020 trial. Lab studies report anti-androgenic and estrogenic activity; the EU has set a concentration limit and required further testing, and it has been measured in coastal waters and coral tissue.

brands: Olay Regenerist Regenerating with Sunscreen Broad Spectrum SPF 15

lead: Homosalate (3,3,5-trimethylcyclohexyl salicylate) is a salicylate ester used as an organic UVB filter in sunscreens and SPF cosmetics [1][2]. It absorbs UVB at roughly 295-315 nm and is reported to be found in about 45% of US sunscreens [2].

It is under scrutiny in Europe for possible endocrine activity. Wikipedia reports a June 2021 SCCS opinion finding no sufficient evidence that pure homosalate is an endocrine disruptor in humans [2], whereas Grokipedia states the committee considered it acceptable only up to 0.5% in certain cosmetics because of unresolved endocrine concerns [1]. The two summaries differ and the primary opinions were not consulted for this article.

paras: Homosalate is a solubilising UVB absorber added to sunscreens and daytime moisturisers, often with avobenzone, octisalate and octocrylene [3]. Labels on such products state they help prevent sunburn and, with other protective measures, decrease the risk of skin cancer and early skin ageing [3].

Wikipedia reports a study in which about 25% of the applied dose reached the stratum corneum on the face, 2-3 times more than on the back, with none detected in volunteers' blood or urine [2]. The 2020 JAMA randomised trial measured homosalate in plasma after sunscreen use among six ingredients [4].

Laboratory work has reported anti-androgenic and estrogenic activity in cell assays [2][5][6][7], and reviews summarise endocrine properties of UV filters [8]. Wikipedia notes no estrogenic effects were seen in several rat and zebrafish experiments and states there is no in vivo evidence of human endocrine toxicity [2].
Homosalate and other UV filters have been measured in Hawaiian coastal water, sediment and coral tissue [9], beaches in the Canary Islands [10], Japanese waters [11], and aquatic biota [12].

Symrise challenged an ECHA decision requiring animal testing of homosalate and octisalate and lost at the Court of Justice of the EU, with orders dated 2021 and 2024 [2]. The EU applies a concentration limit [1].

Clinical research is limited to absorption and allergy. A phase 1 programme enrolled 72 participants [13][4], a 10-person sunscreen SPF study from 2009 is registered [14], and a 1,000-person photopatch study examined photoallergy to sunscreen ingredients [15]. No trial tests homosalate alone for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: JAMA trial reports plasma absorption of homosalate [4].
